How is Calgary's population shared across its communities? It starts with one number: the City of Calgary's own estimate, about one point six million people this November.

Step one. The City's figure comes from its Spring 2026 Economic Outlook, with an estimate for each April. Between those, we draw a straight line, month by month. Right now, that line adds about seventy people a day.
Step two. Each community starts from its own count in the 2021 Census: about one point two nine million people in all. Since then, the City's figure has added about three hundred and nine thousand.

Step three. Where do those people go? About one hundred and eighty thousand live in homes built since 2021, so they are placed in the community where those homes were built. The other one hundred and twenty nine thousand come from more people in each home, seniors' homes, residences, shelters, and people the Census missed. That part is shared by every community: ten percent on top of its 2021 count.

New homes come from the City's property roll. We keep residential accounts with a home on them, and leave out vacant lots, commercial property, parking stalls and storage lockers. A new home counts as lived in one year after it is built, and a rental building counts by its units.

Step four. Every community follows the same rule: its 2021 count, times one point one, plus the people in its new homes. Abbeydale, with no new homes, grows to six thousand five hundred and twenty. Cornerstone, with about thirty two hundred new homes, reaches eighteen thousand one hundred and eighty five. Together, every community adds up to the City's figure.
This is where the new homes are. The most people in new homes are on the edges of the city: Cornerstone, Livingston, Mahogany, Carrington and Seton.
Calgary Data Desk, by Hassan Ali. When the 2026 Census counts arrive in February 2027, every community gets a new starting point.
